title: 08. GraphRAG: Graph Data Structures for RAG
summary: The property graph model is the dominant data structure for Graph RAG systems.

sections.title: ① Concept Explanation
sections.body: The **property graph model** is the dominant data structure for Graph RAG systems. It consists of **nodes** (entities with a label/type and a dictionary of properties), **directed edges** (relationships with a type and their own property dictionary), and optionally **multi-edges** (multiple relationships between the same node pair). Unlike RDF, property graphs allow rich attribute storage directly on both nodes and edges — making them ideal for Graph RAG because entity attributes (description, aliases, confidence) and relationship attributes (weight, source document, timestamp) travel with the graph structure. Neo4j, Memgraph, and Amazon Neptune's Gremlin API all implement property graphs. The model naturally maps to JSON for serialisation and Python dicts for in-memory use.

sections.title: ④ Visual Explanation
sections.body:
```
              GRAPH DATA STRUCTURES FOR RAG — COMPARISON

  PROPERTY GRAPH (Neo4j)          RDF TRIPLE STORE (SPARQL)
  ┌────────────────────────────┐  ┌─────────────────────────────┐
  │                            │  │                             │
  │  [Apple Inc.]              │  │  <Apple_Inc>                │
  │  label: Company            │  │    rdf:type schema:Company  │
  │  props: {                  │  │    schema:name "Apple Inc." │
  │    name: "Apple Inc."      │  │    schema:founded 1976      │
  │    founded: 1976           │  │  .                          │
  │    ticker: "AAPL"          │  │                             │
  │  }                         │  │  <Tim_Cook>                 │
  │      │                     │  │    rdf:type schema:Person   │
  │  EMPLOYS {                 │  │  .                          │
  │    role: "CEO"             │  │                             │
  │    since: "2011"           │  │  <Tim_Cook>                 │
  │  }                         │  │    ex:employedBy <Apple>    │
  │      │                     │  │  .                          │
  │  [Tim Cook]                │  │  ← NO native edge props!   │
  │  label: Person             │  │  Must use reification:     │
  │  props: {name: "Tim Cook"} │  │  _:stmt rdf:subject <TC>   │
  │                            │  │  _:stmt ex:since "2011"    │
  └────────────────────────────┘  └─────────────────────────────┘
           ↓                               ↓
   Fast traversal                  Semantic reasoning
   Rich edge props                 OWL inference
   Cypher/Gremlin                  SPARQL + SPARQL-update
   Best for Graph RAG              Best for linked data

  HYPERGRAPH (3-way+ relationships)
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                    │
  │  Standard Binary Edge:                             │
  │  [Apple] ──ACQUIRED──► [Instagram]    ← OK        │
  │                                                    │
  │  3-way edge (cannot express directly):             │
  │  Apple + Sequoia + Andreessen ──CO-INVESTED──► Stripe │
  │                                                    │
  │  Solution — Reification:                           │
  │  [Apple] ──PARTICIPATED_IN──► [CoInvestEvent_001] │
  │  [Sequoia] ──PARTICIPATED_IN──► [CoInvestEvent_001] │
  │  [a16z] ──PARTICIPATED_IN──► [CoInvestEvent_001]  │
  │  [CoInvestEvent_001] ──TARGET──► [Stripe]         │
  │  [CoInvestEvent_001].amount = $600M               │
  │  [CoInvestEvent_001].date = "2021-03-14"          │
  │                                                    │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  HETEROGENEOUS GRAPH TYPES
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                    │
  │  [Person]──EMPLOYS──►[Company]──PRODUCES──►[Product]│
  │     │                    │                    │    │
  │     │                LOCATED_IN           COMPETES │
  │     │                    │                    │    │
  │  FOUNDED              [Location]          [Company]│
  │     │                                              │
  │  [Company]                                         │
  │                                                    │
  │  ← Multiple node types + edge types = Heterogeneous│
  │  ← Meta-path queries: Person→Company→Fund          │
  │  ← Type constraints prevent nonsensical traversals │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  GRAPH DENSITY vs RAG QUALITY
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                    │
  │  Density = 0.001 (too sparse)                      │
  │  ○ ○   ○ ○   ○   ○ ○ ○   ○                        │
  │  Many isolated nodes → poor retrieval coverage     │
  │                                                    │
  │  Density = 0.05 (optimal for Graph RAG)            │
  │  ○─○─○   ○─○     Power law distribution            │
  │    │ │   │       Few hubs, many leaves             │
  │    ○ ○   ○       Scale-free topology               │
  │                                                    │
  │  Density = 0.5 (too dense, co-occurrence)          │
  │  ●═●═●═●═●═●     Everything connected              │
  │  ║ ║ ║ ║ ║ ║     k-hop explosion → context overflow│
  │  ●═●═●═●═●═●                                       │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

options: JSON-LD — linked data in JSON, widely adopted for web APIs and semantic markup.

An RDF triple is a (subject, predicate, object) statement where ALL three components are URIs (or literals for objects).
quiz.explanation: An RDF triple is a (subject, predicate, object) statement where ALL three components are URIs (or literals for objects). RDF has no built-in mechanism for edge properties — to add metadata to a relationship, you must use reification (creating a new node to represent the statement) or RDF-star extensions.

quiz.explanation: hyperedges** that connect more than two nodes simultaneously. Standard edges are binary (A→B); hyperedges are n-ary (A, B, C, D are all related by a single relationship). In Graph RAG, hyperedges are needed when a single relationship involves multiple entities: a contract between 3 companies, a scientific experiment with multiple authors and subjects, a merger involving acquirer, target, and regulator.

quiz.question: When do you choose a property graph vs RDF for a Graph RAG system?
options: Directed graphs encode asymmetric relationships (Apple ACQUIRED Instagram — not the reverse).
Hybrid schema design: (1) Store entity embeddings as node properties (Neo4j vector index).
Low-density graphs (sparse) have many isolated entities — retrieval finds relevant anchor nodes but the subgraph context is thin.
Choose property graph when: you need rich edge metadata (confidence, timestamps, source docs), you use Cypher/Gremlin queries, you need fast multi-hop traversal, your…
quiz.explanation: Choose property graph when: you need rich edge metadata (confidence, timestamps, source docs), you use Cypher/Gremlin queries, you need fast multi-hop traversal, your team has no RDF/SPARQL expertise.

quiz.question: Explain heterogeneous graphs and their role in Graph RAG.
options: Directed graphs encode asymmetric relationships (Apple ACQUIRED Instagram — not the reverse).
Low-density graphs (sparse) have many isolated entities — retrieval finds relevant anchor nodes but the subgraph context is thin.
Hybrid schema design: (1) Store entity embeddings as node properties (Neo4j vector index).
heterogeneous graph** has multiple node types and multiple edge types, as opposed to homogeneous graphs where all nodes and edges are the same type.
quiz.explanation: heterogeneous graph** has multiple node types and multiple edge types, as opposed to homogeneous graphs where all nodes and edges are the same type. In Graph RAG, knowledge graphs are inherently heterogeneous: nodes can be Person, Company, Product, Location, Event; edges can be EMPLOYS, PRODUCES, LOCATED_IN, ACQUIRED.
